paragraphs: Planning systems often combine neural network predictions with a search over possible actions. When those predictions are wrong, search can be misdirected. This paper asks whether knowing how uncertain the predictions are can help a planner decide where further search is most valuable.

The authors develop a Bayesian planning approach and a tree-search algorithm based on Thompson sampling. They prove a finite-time Bayesian regret bound, describing performance over a limited search horizon rather than only in the long run. They also provide an efficient implementation for a restricted family of posterior distributions and introduce a tree-based variant of Bayes-UCB.

Experiments in ProcGen Maze and Leaper show substantially more effective search when network predictions are inaccurate but their uncertainty estimates are accurate. That condition is central: the finding supports using reliable uncertainty to guide planning, rather than establishing that uncertainty-aware search always helps. The paper also investigates whether commonly used uncertainty estimation methods are accurate enough to deliver meaningful planning gains.
icml-2024-a-bayesian-approach-to-online-.tldr: Bayesian tree search can improve planning when uncertainty estimates reliably identify weaknesses in neural network predictions.

paragraphs: Uncertainty measures for generative models are often designed around a particular task or output type. A technique for language generation may therefore offer little help with images. This paper develops a shared mathematical framework based on kernel scores, which assess outputs through a chosen notion of similarity.

The central contribution separates these scores into bias, variance, and covariance components. From this decomposition, the authors derive kernel-based measures of variance and entropy for estimating uncertainty. They also propose unbiased and consistent estimators that use generated samples without requiring access to the model's internal workings.

The authors demonstrate the framework through generalization and uncertainty experiments involving images, audio, and language. On the CoQA and TriviaQA question-answering datasets, kernel entropy predicts performance better than the evaluated baselines. Because the estimators operate on samples, the approach can also be applied to closed-source models. The contribution connects a theoretical account of generative-model behavior with uncertainty measurements that work across several output domains.
icml-2024-a-bias-variance-covariance-dec.tldr: A kernel-score decomposition yields sample-based uncertainty measures that apply across generative domains and can assess closed-source models.

paragraphs: Mixed-integer linear programming methods need problem instances for development and evaluation, but real application data can be scarce. Generating useful instances requires more than producing different constraints: the resulting problems should retain meaningful characteristics of the originals. Existing approaches that repeatedly modify individual constraints at random can overlook relationships that shape problem quality and solvability.

ACM-MILP addresses this with adaptive selection and coordinated modification. A probability estimate in a learned latent space guides which constraints to change, with the aim of preserving instance characteristics. Community detection identifies strongly related constraints and places them into groups, allowing the generator to modify connected constraints collectively.

Experiments show improved similarity in problem-solving hardness between generated instances and the problems they are intended to resemble. The authors also demonstrate that the generated instances are useful for downstream hyperparameter tuning. These findings support treating constraint dependencies as part of the generation process, particularly when the usefulness of synthetic data depends on preserving computational difficulty.
icml-2024-acm-milp-adaptive-constraint-m.tldr: ACM-MILP generates optimization problems by selecting and modifying related constraints together, improving preservation of solving difficulty.

paragraphs: This paper studies a failure mode in which compromising one multimodal agent can spread harmful behavior through an interacting population. The authors call it infectious jailbreak: after the initial compromise, communication between agents carries the attack onward without further intervention by the adversary.

To test feasibility, the authors simulate populations of up to one million LLaVA-1.5 agents. Their proof-of-concept interaction pattern consists of randomized conversations between pairs. In this setting, placing an infectious adversarial image in the memory of a randomly chosen agent is sufficient to initiate spread, with almost all agents becoming affected exponentially fast.

The result identifies a system-level concern beyond an individual model's response to an adversarial input: agent interaction can propagate an initial failure. Its demonstrated scope is the simulated population and interaction setup described in the study. The authors also derive a principle for deciding whether a defense can provably restrain spread, while leaving the construction of a practical defense satisfying that principle as an open problem.
icml-2024-agent-smith-a-single-image-can.tldr: Simulations show that one adversarial image can trigger rapidly spreading jailbreaks through a large population of interacting multimodal agents.

paragraphs: AI control focuses on preventing harmful outcomes even when a model deliberately tries to cause them. This paper studies that additional layer of defense by designing and testing protocols around an untrusted model. The question is whether a system can benefit from powerful capabilities while resisting attempts to misuse them.

The evaluation setting involves solving a sequence of programming problems without submitting subtly incorrect code. The system has access to a stronger, untrusted GPT-4 model, a weaker, trusted GPT-3.5 model, and a limited amount of high-quality trusted labor. The authors examine multiple protocols and red-team them by developing strategies through which the untrusted model could undermine their safeguards.

Two approaches substantially improve on simple baselines: having the trusted model edit code produced by the untrusted model, and using the untrusted model as a monitor. These findings concern the evaluated programming setup and adversarial strategies. They show that the organization of checking and editing can materially improve safety even when the stronger model itself is not assumed trustworthy.
icml-2024-ai-control-improving-safety-de.tldr: Red-teamed programming protocols improve safety by structuring how trusted and untrusted models edit or monitor code.

paragraphs: A retrieval-augmented language model depends on both the language model and the machinery that retrieves relevant documents. This paper proposes evaluating those choices with an automatically generated multiple-choice exam built from the document collection associated with the task. The exam provides a task-specific basis for comparing system components.

The method uses Item Response Theory to assess exam quality and how much its questions reveal about a model's ability. Questions that provide insufficient information can be removed, allowing the exam to improve iteratively. This makes evaluation itself an object of measurement, rather than treating every generated question as equally useful.

The authors demonstrate the approach on question-answering tasks involving Arxiv abstracts, StackExchange questions, AWS troubleshooting guides, and SEC filings. Their experiments examine model size, retrieval, prompting, and fine-tuning. A notable finding is that selecting an appropriate retrieval algorithm often brings larger gains than increasing language-model size. The reported results support using targeted exams to guide practical RAG design decisions.
icml-2024-automated-evaluation-of-retrie.tldr: Automatically generated, statistically refined exams help compare RAG components and show that retrieval choices often matter more than model size.

paragraphs: Combining causal evidence from multiple data centers becomes difficult when the populations at those centers differ. A common strategy first reweights each site's observed characteristics to resemble a target population, then combines results through meta-analysis. This paper proposes handling the population differences collaboratively within the causal estimator.

The method uses inverse propensity score weighting with weighted propensity models that jointly account for distribution shifts. Instead of making population adjustment a separate site-by-site preprocessing step, it incorporates that adjustment into the collaboration. Federated learning protocols allow the approach to preserve individual-site privacy while enabling the shared estimation procedure.

The authors report significant improvements over meta-analysis-based methods as heterogeneity increases. They also incorporate outcome regression models and prove asymptotic normality when the covariate dimension is below eight. That dimensional condition belongs to the stated theoretical result. Together, the findings support collaborative adjustment as a useful approach to combining heterogeneous evidence, with a distributional guarantee under the specified setting.
icml-2024-collaborative-heterogeneous-ca.tldr: Collaboratively weighted propensity models improve causal estimation across heterogeneous sites, with a stated asymptotic guarantee for covariate dimension below eight.

paragraphs: CRUXEval tests whether a model can reason about what short Python programs do. It contains 800 functions, each three to thirteen lines long and paired with an input and output. The resulting tasks ask a model either to predict the output or to identify an input producing the given output.

The authors provide a model-sampling recipe for creating execution benchmarks, including potentially harder versions. They evaluate twenty code models and find that several recent models with strong HumanEval scores show no corresponding improvement on CRUXEval. This indicates that progress on one code benchmark need not translate into better reasoning about program execution.

Chain-of-thought prompting and fine-tuning improve results but do not solve the benchmark. GPT-4 with chain of thought achieves first-attempt success rates of 75% for input prediction and 81% for output prediction; Code Llama 34B reaches 50% and 46%. Even the strongest evaluated setup repeatedly fails on some simple programs, exposing specific weaknesses that aggregate code-generation performance can miss.
icml-2024-cruxeval-a-benchmark-for-code-.tldr: CRUXEval reveals persistent weaknesses in reasoning about short Python programs, including among models that score highly on code-generation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through repeated denoising, making generation slow. Distillation aims to transfer their behavior into a model requiring far fewer steps. Existing approaches can demand either substantial offline work to produce synthetic training examples or expensive online learning that depends on real data.

BOOT introduces a data-free alternative. It trains a time-conditioned model to predict the pretrained teacher's output from any timestep. Training uses bootstrapping between two consecutive sampled steps, providing an efficient way to learn from the teacher without the data requirements described for prior approaches. The method can also be adapted to large text-to-image models, whose original training collections may be difficult to access.

On several benchmark datasets in the DDIM setting, BOOT achieves generation quality comparable to the diffusion teacher while being orders of magnitude faster. Its text-to-image results also demonstrate the ability to handle complex distributions. The contribution is both a faster generation model and a training procedure that reduces the practical burden of obtaining that model.
icml-2024-data-free-distillation-of-diff.tldr: BOOT uses data-free bootstrapping to distill diffusion teachers into much faster generators with comparable quality in the reported DDIM experiments.

paragraphs: DS-Agent addresses a weakness of language-model agents for data science: they can propose unreasonable experiments when trying to select and train suitable models. The framework uses case-based reasoning, drawing on previous solutions and expert knowledge to guide how an agent approaches a new task.

During development, DS-Agent organizes work into an iterative process informed by Kaggle expertise and experimental feedback. During deployment, it uses a simpler process that adapts successful development-stage solutions directly into code. Reusing those cases reduces the demands placed on the underlying language model and supports a lower-resource deployment stage.

In the reported evaluation, DS-Agent with GPT-4 achieves a 100% development-stage success rate. Across alternative language models, deployment shows a 36% improvement in average one-pass rate. DS-Agent also receives the best performance rank in both stages, with reported GPT-4 costs of $1.60 per development run and $0.13 per deployment run. These results support grounding automated experimentation in reusable cases and feedback within the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-ds-agent-automated-data-scienc.tldr: DS-Agent combines language models with reusable expert cases and feedback to improve automated data science while lowering deployment costs.

paragraphs: Incomplete multi-view clustering groups examples described through several kinds of information when some of those views are missing. EDISON combines missing-data inference with representations designed to capture relationships within and across views. Its goal is to maintain useful clustering structure without making computation prohibitively expensive.

The method begins with an enhanced dictionary representation, which supports both estimating missing information and building anchor graphs. It then introduces Gaussian error rank as an approximation to tensor rank. This component is intended to account for information carried by different singular values in the tensor representation, rather than overlooking their varied contributions.

EDISON also adds a hyper-anchor graph Laplacian regularizer that brings together higher-order relationships across views and local relationships within each view. These components connect efficient representation, recovery of missing information, and preservation of relational structure. Extensive experiments report better effectiveness and efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined design for the incomplete multi-view clustering problems evaluated.
icml-2024-edison-enhanced-dictionary-ind.tldr: EDISON combines dictionary representations, tensor-rank approximation, and graph regularization to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of incomplete multi-view clustering.

paragraphs: Broad category labels are often easier to obtain than labels distinguishing closely related classes. This paper asks how to use those broad labels to discover finer categories without receiving examples labeled at the finer level. FALCON is designed to extract that additional structure from coarsely labeled data.

The method jointly infers the unknown fine-grained classes and their relationships to the available coarse classes. Learning both together addresses two linked uncertainties: which detailed categories exist and how they fit into the broader labeling scheme. Its modular design also allows it to learn from multiple datasets that use different labeling strategies.

The authors evaluate FALCON on eight image classification tasks and one single-cell classification task. It outperforms the compared baselines by substantial margins, including a reported 22% improvement over the strongest baseline on tieredImageNet, which contains more than 600 fine-grained classes. These results show that coarse supervision can support discovering much more detailed class structure in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-fine-grained-classes-and-how-t.tldr: FALCON discovers fine-grained classes and their relationships to coarse labels without fine-grained supervision.

paragraphs: Neural networks are often trained successfully despite having complicated, nonconvex loss landscapes. This paper investigates the geometry encountered along actual training paths, focusing on sampled gradients. The aim is to explain efficient optimization through properties of the trajectories that training follows.

The analysis examines the restricted secant inequality, an error bound, and their ratio, gamma. These quantities describe aspects of the geometry relevant to first-order optimization. Across the reported experiments, they behave predictably and consistently despite minibatch randomness. The observations suggest that trajectories avoid significant obstacles and retain stable dynamics through most of training.

The observed properties are sufficient to establish linear convergence theoretically and to motivate learning-rate schedules resembling practical choices. Experiments span image classification, semantic segmentation, and language modeling while varying architectures, batch sizes, datasets, optimizers, and initialization seeds. The contribution connects measured training-path geometry to convergence theory; the empirical regularities and sufficient theoretical conditions should not be read as an unconditional guarantee for every neural-network training run.
icml-2024-no-wrong-turns-the-simple-geom.tldr: Measured geometry along neural-network training paths exhibits regularities that support linear-convergence theory and practical learning-rate schedules.

paragraphs: Many learning problems require understanding how a solution changes when a parameter changes, even when that solution is defined by repeatedly applying a map until it settles. This paper studies derivatives of such fixed points when the map is a contraction but is not differentiable. Nonsmoothness makes the usual chain-rule reasoning unavailable.

The authors analyze iterative differentiation, which differentiates through successive iterations, and approximate implicit differentiation, which works through the fixed-point relationship. Building on prior nonsmooth analysis under a piecewise Lipschitz smooth assumption, they establish a linear rate for approximate implicit differentiation and improve the deterministic rate for iterative differentiation. These rates closely match those available in smooth settings.

They also introduce NSID for a stochastic setting where the contraction combines an outer map with an inner map available only through an unbiased stochastic estimator. Its convergence guarantees encompass the best available smooth-setting rates. Illustrative experiments support the analysis, extending tools relevant to hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and other applications involving parameter-dependent solutions.
icml-2024-nonsmooth-implicit-differentia.tldr: The paper establishes improved nonsmooth fixed-point differentiation rates and introduces a stochastic method with guarantees encompassing leading smooth-setting rates.

paragraphs: A human pose estimator predicts body-keypoint locations and confidence values. For confidence to be useful, it should reflect how accurate those predictions are. This paper shows through theory and experiments that common confidence heuristics, such as taking a heatmap's maximum value, leave a gap between reported confidence and pose accuracy.

The theoretical analysis leads to explicit confidence adjustments using additionally inferred instance size and visibility. These factors supply information that a simple heatmap-based confidence can miss. However, the authors find that such closed-form adjustments alone cannot eliminate the calibration gap because they cannot fully account for the behavior of a black-box neural network.

To address the remaining mismatch, the authors introduce Calibrated ConfidenceNet, or CCNet. It adds a confidence-prediction branch that learns adjustments specific to the underlying network. As a lightweight component applied after the original model is available, CCNet improves calibration in standard off-the-shelf pose estimators. The stated improvement concerns making confidence more faithful to prediction accuracy.
icml-2024-on-the-calibration-of-human-po.tldr: CCNet improves pose-estimation confidence calibration by combining analytically motivated adjustments with learned network-specific corrections.

paragraphs: When a neural network learns tasks in sequence, learning a new task can damage its performance on earlier ones. This is catastrophic forgetting. Earlier empirical work found that making networks wider can reduce forgetting, but it did not precisely characterize how the benefit changes as width grows.

This paper develops a theoretical framework for continual learning and analyzes the connection between width and forgetting in feed-forward networks. The key result is diminishing returns: additional width can reduce forgetting, but the benefit of further increases becomes smaller. This gives a more informative account of scaling than the observation that wider networks tend to forget less.

The authors test the prediction at widths beyond those explored in prior studies and observe the diminishing returns anticipated by their theory. The combined analysis and experiments explain why width can be useful while becoming progressively less effective as a remedy. The stated theoretical scope is feed-forward networks, with empirical evidence supporting the predicted trend at the examined widths.
icml-2024-on-the-diminishing-returns-of-.tldr: Theory and experiments show that increasing feed-forward network width reduces continual-learning forgetting with diminishing returns.

paragraphs: Simply enlarging a recommendation model does not necessarily produce substantial performance gains. This paper identifies embedding collapse as an obstacle: the learned embedding matrix occupies a low-dimensional subspace, so a larger representation may still express limited diversity. The authors investigate this behavior through both theory and experiments.

Their analysis finds that feature interactions have two competing effects. Interacting with collapsed embeddings can constrain learning and worsen collapse. Yet interactions also help prevent the model from fitting spurious features, making them important for scalability. The resulting design challenge is to retain useful interactions while reducing their contribution to collapse.

The proposed solution learns multiple embedding sets, each with its own interaction module. This arrangement aims to keep the sets diverse and thereby reduce collapse. Extensive experiments report consistent scalability and effective collapse mitigation across several recommendation models. The findings connect poor scaling to the structure of learned representations and support changing how embeddings interact as a route to more useful model growth.
icml-2024-on-the-embedding-collapse-when.tldr: Multiple diverse embedding sets with separate interaction modules reduce embedding collapse and improve recommendation-model scalability in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Density-ratio estimation uses samples to estimate how two probability distributions differ at a given point. This paper identifies a limitation in a broad class of kernel-based estimators: their error convergence can saturate. On highly regular problems, that saturation prevents the methods from achieving the faster error rates the problem structure could otherwise support.

The proposed remedy is iterated regularization. The authors introduce it into density-ratio estimation to overcome the saturation effect and obtain fast error rates. The contribution therefore concerns how an estimator benefits from favorable problem structure, rather than only whether it can produce a usable ratio estimate.

Experiments compare the proposed methods with their counterparts using non-iterative regularization. The iterated versions perform better on density-ratio benchmarks and in large-scale evaluations of importance-weighted ensembles of deep unsupervised domain adaptation models. These evaluations connect the estimation result to a downstream use of density ratios. Together, the findings support repeated regularization as a way to address a specific convergence bottleneck with practical consequences.
icml-2024-overcoming-saturation-in-densi.tldr: Iterated regularization overcomes error-rate saturation in kernel density-ratio estimation and improves the reported estimation and domain-adaptation results.

paragraphs: A proposed predictive policy is often justified by claiming it will outperform the current decision process. That comparison is difficult when the existing policy is incompletely specified or depends on unobserved factors. This paper develops a way to compare policies while retaining uncertainty about those factors.

The key insight is that some uncertain regions can be safely ignored for the comparison, even if they matter for characterizing policies individually. The framework accommodates several causal identification approaches, including instrumental variables, marginal sensitivity models, and proximal variables. It estimates finite-sample regret intervals without assuming a particular parametric form for the status quo policy.

Those intervals express uncertainty in comparative predictive performance instead of forcing a single fully determined answer. The authors verify the framework theoretically and through synthetic-data experiments, then apply it to evaluating a proposed healthcare enrollment-policy change before deployment. The contribution makes comparison possible under multiple identification approaches while avoiding a specific structural assumption about the existing policy; it does not remove the assumptions attached to those approaches.
icml-2024-predictive-performance-compari.tldr: The framework estimates policy-performance differences under confounding by ignoring uncertainty irrelevant to the comparison and reporting regret intervals.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often produces one behavior specialized for a particular task. Quality-Diversity Actor-Critic, or QDAC, instead aims to learn a collection of behaviors that are both effective and varied. Such a collection can provide useful alternatives when the conditions facing an agent change.

QDAC is an off-policy actor-critic method with two critics: a value-function critic and a successor-features critic. Its actor uses a constrained optimization objective that brings the two together, pursuing high return while executing diverse skills. This makes behavioral diversity part of the learning objective alongside task performance.

Across six continuous-control locomotion tasks, QDAC achieves significantly higher performance and greater behavioral diversity than the compared quality-diversity methods. The authors also use the learned skills in five perturbed environments, where they support better adaptation than the evaluated baselines. These results connect the training objective to both a richer set of behaviors and improved responses to changed conditions in the tested environments.
icml-2024-quality-diversity-actor-critic.tldr: QDAC combines value and successor-features critics to learn diverse, high-performing skills that improve adaptation in tested perturbed environments.

paragraphs: Studying deep learning can require substantial computation, even when the goal is to understand a basic training phenomenon. MNIST-1D is a small, procedurally generated benchmark intended to make such investigations faster and cheaper. Its examples have only 40 dimensions, and the default training set contains 4,000 examples.

Despite that small scale, the authors show that the benchmark supports several distinct investigations. These include comparing architectural inductive biases, finding lottery tickets, observing deep double descent, learning an activation function through meta-learning, and demonstrating guillotine regularization in self-supervised learning. The value is that a compact problem still exhibits a range of behaviors researchers want to study.

The reported experiments run within minutes on a GPU and often on a CPU. That makes repeated experimentation accessible for prototyping, teaching, and research with limited resources. The paper's contribution is a concrete demonstration that several substantive deep-learning questions can be explored at small scale, reducing the cost of investigating those particular phenomena.
icml-2024-scaling-down-deep-learning-wit.tldr: MNIST-1D makes several deep-learning phenomena practical to study within minutes using a tiny, procedurally generated dataset.

paragraphs: SLAB targets two computational bottlenecks in efficient transformers: normalization and attention. Layer normalization requires statistics to be calculated during inference, adding computational cost. Batch normalization offers a more efficient alternative, but directly substituting it can degrade performance or cause training to collapse.

The proposed PRepBN method makes the replacement progressively during training, moving from layer normalization to re-parameterized batch normalization. The authors pair this with a simplified linear-attention module. Together, these changes address both the cost of normalization and the expense of attention while aiming to preserve model performance.

Experiments on image classification and object detection support the approach. SLAB-Swin reaches 83.6% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 16.2-millisecond latency, reported as 2.4 milliseconds faster and 0.1 percentage point more accurate than Flatten-Swin. Language-modeling experiments also show comparable performance with lower latency. The findings support addressing normalization alongside attention when improving transformer efficiency, with the measured gains applying to the evaluated models and tasks.
icml-2024-slab-efficient-transformers-wi.tldr: SLAB combines progressive normalization replacement with simplified linear attention to reduce transformer latency while preserving strong performance.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized density means generating examples when the target distribution is specified without its normalizing constant. This paper approaches that problem through stochastic localization, where a stochastic observation process adds noise and an associated denoiser describes how to recover information about the underlying sample.

The authors introduce an explicit family of observation processes with flexible denoising schedules. Their complete sampling method, SLIPS, approximately samples the resulting dynamics and thereby obtains samples from the target distribution. A central component is estimating the denoiser using Markov chain Monte Carlo, connecting the localization process to a practical posterior-sampling procedure.

The paper also supplies implementation guidance and illustrates SLIPS on several multimodal sampling benchmarks. These include Gaussian mixtures of increasing dimension, Bayesian logistic regression, and a high-dimensional statistical-mechanics field system. The examples demonstrate benefits and applicability across different distributional settings. The contribution extends stochastic localization toward a general sampling task while providing a concrete procedure for approximating the required dynamics.
icml-2024-stochastic-localization-via-it.tldr: SLIPS uses Monte Carlo denoiser estimates within stochastic localization to approximately sample unnormalized target distributions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can perform well empirically while leaving open which structural differences they can recognize. This paper studies that question for networks built around paths. Its focus is expressive power: the graph distinctions a method can represent, beyond its performance on a particular prediction task.

The authors introduce PATH-WL, a family of color-refinement algorithms using paths and shortest-path distances. Color refinement assigns and updates structural labels to distinguish parts of a graph. The theoretical analysis shows that PATH-WL can count cycles and is incomparable with a broad range of expressive graph neural networks. Incomparability means neither side uniformly subsumes the other's distinguishing capabilities.

Experiments also show strong results on strongly regular graphs, a family identified as particularly difficult. Together, the theoretical and empirical findings indicate that path-based information supports a distinct hierarchy of highly expressive graph models. The contribution is therefore a systematic account of what path-based methods can distinguish, with experimental evidence on a demanding graph family.
icml-2024-the-expressive-power-of-path-b.tldr: PATH-WL establishes a path-based expressiveness hierarchy with cycle-counting abilities and capabilities incomparable to many existing graph neural networks.

paragraphs: VQ-MTM adapts BERT-style self-supervised learning to EEG time series. Its central challenge is producing useful learning units from signals that may be corrupted and periodic. The method constructs discrete semantic units analogous to words, giving masked time-series modeling more consistent targets.

Two modules support that representation. A theoretically grounded random-projection quantization module creates the discrete units, while a phase-alignment module uses the Fourier transform's relationship between time shifts and phase shifts. Together, they are designed to provide robust, consistent learning signals despite the signal properties that complicate EEG modeling.

The authors describe the model as having low complexity and being readily adaptable to large datasets. They evaluate it on five real-world datasets, including two large-scale datasets, and report consistently substantial gains over existing methods on seizure detection and classification tasks. These findings support the combination of quantization and phase alignment as a useful basis for self-supervised EEG learning in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-vector-quantization-pretrainin.tldr: VQ-MTM combines random-projection quantization and phase alignment to improve self-supervised EEG learning and reported seizure-task performance.
